countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The buying and selling of goods, or a skilled job learned by training.
examples: *Trade* between the two countries has doubled since 2019.
He learned a *trade* instead of going to college.
The new tariffs hurt small shops that live on cross-border *trade*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A branch of business that makes one kind of product, or manufacturing as a whole.
examples: She spent twenty years in the music *industry*.
Heavy *industry* still employs a lot of people up north.
Several *industries* were hit hard by the shutdown.

gloss: A large business that the law treats as a single person.
examples: The *corporation* moved its head office to Texas.
Big *corporations* pay far less tax than most people think.
She left a huge *corporation* to run a bakery.

gloss: A company, especially one that sells professional services.
examples: He works for a law *firm* downtown.
The *firm* has offices in six cities.
Two accounting *firms* bid on the audit.

gloss: A new company, usually small and aiming to grow fast.
examples: He quit a steady job to join a *startup*.
Most *startups* run out of money in the first two years.
The *startup* raised eight million dollars last spring.

gloss: A building where goods are made by machine in large numbers.
examples: Her father worked at the *factory* for thirty years.
The *factory* runs three shifts a day.
Half the *factories* along the river closed in the nineties.

gloss: A large building where goods are stored before they are sold or shipped.
examples: Your order is still sitting in the *warehouse* in Memphis.
They rented a *warehouse* out by the airport.
Both *warehouses* are full through the holidays.

gloss: A room or building where people do desk work for a company.
examples: Stop by my *office* after lunch.
They opened a second *office* in Denver.
Most of our *offices* are half empty on Fridays.

gloss: A local office or store belonging to a larger company or bank.
examples: The bank closed the *branch* on Main Street.
You can pick it up at any *branch*.
They're opening two new *branches* this year.
contrast: Americans say BRANCH with the vowel of cat; the British use a long ah sound.

gloss: The right to run a business under a big company's name, or a store run that way.
examples: He bought a pizza *franchise* in Tulsa.
The *franchise* costs about two hundred thousand up front.
There are over forty *franchises* in the state.

gloss: A business owned by two or more people, or a working tie between companies.
examples: The two of them formed a *partnership* right out of school.
The *partnership* fell apart over money.
We have *partnerships* with three local farms.

gloss: The joining of two companies into one.
examples: The *merger* was announced Monday morning.
A lot of people lost their jobs after the *merger*.
Regulators blocked two *mergers* last year.

gloss: The legal state of not being able to pay what you owe.
examples: The chain filed for *bankruptcy* in March.
*Bankruptcy* wiped out most of his debt.
Small-business *bankruptcies* are up this quarter.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Rivalry between sellers, or an organized contest.
examples: There's a lot of *competition* in the coffee business.
We keep an eye on what the *competition* is charging.
She won a baking *competition* at the state fair.

gloss: A senior person who helps run a company and makes the big decisions.
examples: The *executive* who hired me is retiring.
Three *executives* resigned in the same week.
She's an *executive* at a software company.

gloss: Someone who starts a business and takes on the risk of running it.
examples: He's been an *entrepreneur* since he was nineteen.
The city runs a program for young *entrepreneurs*.
Every *entrepreneur* I know has failed at something.

gloss: Someone who puts money into a business or property hoping to earn more back.
examples: An *investor* from Chicago put up half the money.
*Investors* pulled out as soon as the news broke.
We're pitching to a group of *investors* on Thursday.

gloss: Someone who owns shares in a company.
examples: Every *shareholder* gets a vote.
*Shareholders* meet in April.
He's the largest *shareholder* in the company.

gloss: A company that provides goods or materials to another company.
examples: Our main *supplier* raised prices again.
We switched *suppliers* after the delays.
The *supplier* ships out of Ohio.

gloss: A person or company that sells something, especially to a business or on the street.
examples: A street *vendor* was selling hot dogs on the corner.
We pay our *vendors* within thirty days.
The software *vendor* handles all the updates.

gloss: A business that sells goods directly to the public.
examples: The *retailer* is closing forty stores.
Online *retailers* took most of the holiday traffic.
We sell through one big *retailer* and our own site.

gloss: A company that makes goods in large quantities.
examples: The *manufacturer* covers the parts for two years.
Most of these *manufacturers* are overseas.
Call the *manufacturer* before you take it apart.

gloss: Someone who buys something, or whose job is buying stock for a store.
examples: The house had three *buyers* interested in one weekend.
She's a *buyer* for a department store.
We finally found a *buyer* for the truck.

gloss: A person who buys and uses goods and services.
examples: *Consumers* are spending less on eating out.
The law gives the *consumer* thirty days to return it.
American *consumers* drove most of the growth last year.
contrast: Americans say kun-SOO-mur; the British add a y sound: kun-SYOO-mur.

gloss: The series of jobs a person holds over a working life.
examples: She spent her whole *career* in banking.
Teaching is a good *career* if you can live with the pay.
Both *careers* took off after they moved west.
contrast: Don't mix up *career* (kuh-REER) with carrier (KA-ree-ur), a company that hauls freight.
